gloss_terse: Royal delicacy; choice food from the king's table, a Persian loanword used exclusively in Daniel
gloss_readable: A Persian loanword (cf. Sanskrit prati-bhaga, 'a portion') denoting the fine food and delicacies served at the royal table. It appears only in Daniel, where the young captives are offered the king's provisions but choose to abstain. The multilingual evidence is remarkably unified: Spanish 'comida del rey,' English 'delicacy,' and French 'nourriture' all point to a single, clear meaning. The word captures not just the food itself but the political and spiritual implications of accepting a foreign king's bounty.

senses.1: Royal delicacy or choice food portioned from the king's own table. Used exclusively in the book of Daniel (1:5, 8, 13, 15, 16; 11:26) for the provisions offered to the captive Judean youths and later for the food of those who eat at a ruler's table. The Persian origin underscores the Babylonian court setting. Multilingual translations converge tightly: Spanish 'comida del rey,' English 'delicacy,' French 'nourriture' — all confirming a single semantic field of royal provisions.

gloss_terse: Suddenly, in an instant; denotes unexpected, abrupt occurrence
gloss_readable: An adverb expressing sudden, unexpected action — something that happens without warning or preparation. Often paired with the near-synonym pitʾom for emphatic force ('very suddenly,' Num 6:9). It appears in legal contexts for accidental harm (Num 35:22), in prophetic oracles for swift divine judgment (Isa 29:5; 30:13; Hab 2:7), and in wisdom literature for the abrupt ruin of the fool (Prov 6:15; 29:1). Spanish 'de repente' and 'subitamente' confirm the consistent meaning across all occurrences.

senses.1: Suddenly, in an instant — marking an action or event as abrupt and unforeseen. In Numbers 35:22 it qualifies an accidental thrust ('in suddenness,' i.e., without premeditation). Paired with pitʾom in Numbers 6:9 and Isaiah 29:5 for emphatic force ('very suddenly'). In Proverbs 6:15 and 29:1 it describes the swift, irreversible breaking of the fool. Multilingual glosses are unanimous: Spanish 'de repente / subitamente,' English 'in a moment / in an instant,' all pointing to one clear temporal adverb.

gloss_terse: To heap up, accumulate, store in great quantity
gloss_readable: A verb meaning to pile up or accumulate something in abundance. Its most memorable use is Joseph heaping up grain 'like the sand of the sea' during Egypt's seven years of plenty (Gen 41:35, 49). It also describes the Israelites heaping dead frogs after the plague (Exod 8:14), Tyre heaping silver like dust (Zech 9:3), and the futility of the wicked who heap up riches they will never enjoy (Job 27:16; Ps 39:6). The cognate Arabic dabara ('collect, bind together') confirms the core gathering-and-piling semantics.

senses.1: To heap up, pile, or store in great quantity — emphasizing the sheer volume of what is accumulated. Joseph stored grain beyond measure during the plentiful years (Gen 41:35, 49). The Israelites heaped up dead frogs in stinking piles (Exod 8:14). Habakkuk 1:10 speaks of heaping up dust against a fortified city. In wisdom contexts, the verb carries an ironic edge: the wicked heap silver like dust (Job 27:16; Zech 9:3) or store up wealth that others will spend (Ps 39:6). Spanish 'acumular / amontonar' and English 'heap up / store' confirm the single, consistent sense.

gloss_terse: Zoan — ancient Egyptian city (Tanis) in the Nile Delta, seat of Pharaoh's court
gloss_readable: The Hebrew name for the ancient Egyptian city of Tanis (Greek), located in the northeastern Nile Delta. Scripture remembers it as the place where God performed wonders before Pharaoh (Ps 78:12, 43) and as a seat of Egyptian power whose counselors Isaiah mocks as fools (Isa 19:11, 13; 30:4). Numbers 13:22 notes that Hebron was built seven years before Zoan, using it as a chronological benchmark for great antiquity. The modern site is San el-Hagar in Egypt.

senses.1: Zoan (Tanis) — a proper noun identifying the major Egyptian city in the northeastern Nile Delta that served as a royal capital. Psalm 78:12 and 43 recall it as the 'field of Zoan' where God wrought signs and wonders during the Exodus. Isaiah 19:11 and 13 mock the princes of Zoan for their foolish counsel, and 30:4 names it alongside Hanes as a destination for Judah's ill-fated embassy to Egypt. Numbers 13:22 uses its founding date as a reference point for Hebron's antiquity. Multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate: English 'Zoan,' Spanish 'Zoán,' French 'Zoan.'

gloss_terse: Zippor — personal name, father of Balak king of Moab; meaning 'bird' or 'sparrow'
gloss_readable: A masculine proper name meaning 'bird' (perhaps specifically 'sparrow'), borne by the father of Balak, king of Moab, who hired Balaam to curse Israel. The name appears seven times, always identifying Balak's lineage (Num 22:2, 4, 10, 16; 23:18; Josh 24:9; Judg 11:25). The bird-name follows a common Semitic pattern of animal names for persons, paralleled by the Palmyrene name Tsipra. All translations simply transliterate: English, Spanish, French, and German all render 'Zippor.'

senses.1: Zippor — a proper name ('bird, sparrow') identifying the father of Balak, king of Moab. Every occurrence (Num 22:2, 4, 10, 16; 23:18; Josh 24:9; Judg 11:25) appears in the patronymic formula 'Balak son of Zippor,' establishing Balak's royal lineage in the context of Moab's attempt to have Israel cursed by Balaam. The name reflects the common ancient Near Eastern practice of using animal names for persons (cf. Palmyrene Tsipra). All multilingual glosses uniformly transliterate the name without translation.

gloss_terse: A small jug or flask for carrying water or oil, used in the Saul-David and Elijah narratives
gloss_readable: A feminine noun denoting a small, flat-bodied jug or flask used for holding water or oil. In the David-and-Saul narratives, it is the water jug David snatched from beside the sleeping king's head as proof of his mercy (1 Sam 26:11, 12, 16). In the Elijah cycle, it is the widow of Zarephath's oil jar that miraculously never runs dry (1 Kgs 17:12, 14, 16) and the water cruse left by the angel at Elijah's head (1 Kgs 19:6). Spanish 'vasija' and English 'jug/flask' confirm a single concrete referent.

senses.1: A small jug, flask, or cruse — a portable vessel of flat or broad shape used to carry water or oil. In 1 Samuel 26:11, 12, and 16, it is the water jug that David took from beside Saul's sleeping head in the wilderness of Ziph, demonstrating his refusal to harm the Lord's anointed. In 1 Kings 17:12, 14, and 16, it is the widow's oil jar that was miraculously sustained during the famine, and in 1 Kings 19:6 it is the water cruse placed at Elijah's head by the angel. Spanish 'vasija/jarra,' English 'jug/jar' — the glosses consistently point to a single small household vessel.

gloss_terse: Qohelet — 'the Preacher' or 'the Assembler'; title of the author-speaker in Ecclesiastes
gloss_readable: A title meaning 'one who assembles' or 'one who convenes,' traditionally rendered 'the Preacher' (following Jerome's concionator and the Greek Ekklesiastes). The feminine morphology likely indicates an office or function rather than gender — comparable to Arabic khalifa ('caliph'). Used exclusively in Ecclesiastes (1:1, 2, 12; 7:27; 12:8, 9, 10) to identify the book's speaker, who is presented as a royal sage in Jerusalem. Whether the emphasis falls on assembling people (a convener) or assembling wisdom sayings (a collector) has been debated since antiquity.

senses.1: Qohelet — a functional title designating the speaker of the book of Ecclesiastes, meaning either 'one who convenes an assembly' or 'one who collects (wisdom sayings).' The Greek translation Ekklesiastes and Jerome's concionator both favor the 'preacher/convener' reading, while the Hebrew root qahal ('to assemble') and the reference to 'collected proverbs' in Eccl 12:9-11 support the 'collector' sense. The feminine form likely denotes office rather than gender (cf. sophereth, Ezra 2:55). Appears in Eccl 1:1, 2, 12; 7:27; 12:8, 9, 10. French 'assemblée' and Spanish 'Qohélet' reflect the two translation strategies — functional rendering versus transliteration.

gloss_terse: Sound, voice (Aramaic); used in Daniel for audible proclamations and the sound of instruments
gloss_readable: The Aramaic noun for 'sound' or 'voice,' cognate with Hebrew qol. In Daniel it serves double duty: it denotes the sound of musical instruments that signal the moment to bow before Nebuchadnezzar's golden image (Dan 3:5, 7, 10, 15), and it refers to a spoken voice — the heavenly voice that announces judgment on Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 4:31) and the king's own voice calling out to Daniel in the lions' den (Dan 6:20). Spanish distinguishes 'sonido de' (sound of instruments) from 'voz' (spoken voice), neatly reflecting the word's dual application.

senses.1: Sound or voice — the Aramaic counterpart of Hebrew qol, covering both instrumental sound and spoken voice. In Daniel 3:5, 7, 10, and 15, it appears in construct ('sound of the horn, pipe, lyre...') for the musical signal commanding worship of the golden image. In Daniel 4:31 it is the heavenly voice that falls upon Nebuchadnezzar announcing the loss of his kingdom, and in 6:20 it is the king's anxious voice calling to Daniel. Spanish helpfully distinguishes 'sonido de' for instrumental sound and 'voz' for spoken voice, though the Aramaic word covers both with a single form.

gloss_terse: Ice, frost; frozen water as a natural phenomenon of cold weather
gloss_readable: A noun denoting ice or frost — frozen water in its natural forms. Jacob invokes the nighttime frost that consumed him during his years with Laban (Gen 31:40). Job and the Psalms celebrate it as a manifestation of God's sovereign power over creation: water hardens like stone (Job 37:10), ice has a mysterious origin (Job 38:29), and God hurls his ice like morsels (Ps 147:17). Ezekiel 1:22 uses the word to describe the awesome expanse above the living creatures, 'gleaming like ice.' Spanish 'hielo' and English 'ice/frost' confirm the unified semantic range.

senses.1: Ice or frost — frozen water as a natural meteorological phenomenon. Used in Genesis 31:40 for the bitter nighttime frost Jacob endured, in Jeremiah 36:30 for winter cold, and extensively in wisdom poetry: Job 6:16 (dark with ice), Job 37:10 (water frozen solid by God's breath), Job 38:29 (the womb of ice as divine mystery), and Psalm 147:17 (God hurling ice like morsels). Ezekiel 1:22 applies it figuratively to the gleaming, crystalline expanse above the cherubim. Spanish 'hielo,' English 'ice/frost,' French 'glace' — multilingual glosses consistently point to the single domain of frozen water.

gloss_terse: Hostility, contrariness; opposition to God expressed as walking 'contrary' to him
gloss_readable: A noun meaning 'opposition' or 'contrariness,' used exclusively in Leviticus 26 in the idiom 'to walk in hostility with' someone. It describes the stubborn, defiant posture of Israel toward God — and God's corresponding response in kind. The chapter's escalating curses hinge on this word: if Israel walks contrary to God (vv. 21, 23, 27, 40), God will walk contrary to them (vv. 24, 28, 41). The sevenfold repetition in a single chapter underscores its rhetorical weight as the defining word for covenant defiance.

senses.1: Hostility, contrariness, or opposition — a disposition of walking 'against' or 'contrary to' God, used only in the covenant-curse discourse of Leviticus 26. Israel is warned: if you walk with me in qeri (hostility, Lev 26:21, 23, 27, 40), then I will walk with you in qeri (vv. 24, 28, 41), even 'in the fury of qeri' (v. 28). The word captures not mere disobedience but a persistent, defiant contrariness — a deliberate refusal to yield. Multilingual glosses (English 'hostility,' Spanish 'hostilidad,' French 'hostilité') consistently render it as opposition, though the Hebrew nuance of 'contrariwise' — doing the opposite of what is asked — is difficult to capture in a single word.
